Flaring Middle East Tensions Push Oil Prices Up
 
Plus, bond yields rise and Amazon faces a new legal challenge
 
By Heard on the Street Staff
 
 
REUTERS
 

This is an edition of the Markets P.M. newsletter, a recap of the day’s most important markets moves, delivered after the closing bell. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

What Happened in Markets Today

 

Oil is back up. Iran and the U.S. traded strikes in the Middle East, pushing Brent crude futures above $90—right about where they started this month. A U.S. attack on Sunday—the first in about a month targeting Iran—hit missile launchers on an island in the Strait of Hormuz. Shortly thereafter, missiles were fired at Jordan, where the U.S. has significant military assets.

 

Long-dated bond yields are rising. Yields on 10-year Treasury notes are near their highest levels since January 2025, while yields on longer-dated government bonds in Europe are also edging higher. The rises reflect the geopolitical uncertainty and concerns about inflation heading into September’s Fed meeting. The market-implied probability of an interest-rate hike was around 66% Monday, up from about 41% a week earlier.

 

California utility stocks nosedived. Two major utilities that have a lot to lose if they can be held liable for wildfire damage fell sharply Monday. The moves followed lawmakers’ rejection of Gov. Gavin Newsom’s call to block insurers from suing the utilities over wildfire claims—a provision he argued was necessary to keep consumer prices down. PG&E’s stock fell 20%, while Edison International fell 23%.

 

Major stock indexes ended lower. The S&P 500 fell 0.3%, and the Nasdaq was off 0.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 374 points, or 0.7%.

One Big Story

 
 
KLAUS GALIANO/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

The Federal Trade Commission is suing Amazon.com, alleging the tech and retail giant deceived advertisers. Amazon, the FTC alleges, made tens of billions of dollars selling ads in an auction system that it manipulated to raise prices advertisers paid.

 

The case adds to Amazon’s substantial legal headaches, including a monopolization case filed in 2023 and headed to trial next year. The company also agreed to pay $2.5 billion to settle FTC allegations that it tricked customers into signing up for its Prime service and made it hard to cancel.

 

News of the new case sent Amazon’s shares 2.5% lower on Monday.

 
 
 

What’s Coming Up

 

• New data on U.S. manufacturing growth in August are expected Tuesday morning.

 

• U.S. construction spending figures for July are also due.

 

• Cybersecurity player Palo Alto Networks and computing-equipment maker Dell report quarterly results after the bell Tuesday.
